title: The Boycott
year: 7th to 10th year of prophethood — c. 616 to 619 CE
teaser: A document hung on the wall of the Ka'bah sealed two clans into a valley. Three years. Leaves and skins.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A starvation order hung on the Ka'bah wall
layers.content:
Every plot had failed. Assault, ridicule, bribery, the attempt to strangle him at prayer — each one had been tried and each one had run out. And around the Prophet ﷺ the two clans of Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib had closed ranks. Abu Talib had put the question to them plainly and they answered him: believer and idolater alike, they would shield the man. Only Abu Lahab broke from his own blood and went over to the other side.

So Quraysh stopped attacking the man and attacked the shelter. They met at Khaif Banu Kinanah, at a place called Wadi Al-Muhassab, and formed a confederation against both clans. They swore an oath together: no buying or selling with them, no marriage into them, no visiting, no sitting with them, no word spoken to them in the street — until Muhammad ﷺ was handed over to be killed.

Then they wrote it down. Ibn Al-Qayyim records that the reports disagree over whose hand held the pen — some name Mansur bin Ikrimah, some Nadr bin Al-Harith, and the sounder view is Bagheed bin Amir. It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ supplicated against him and that his writing hand was later paralysed.

The parchment was affixed to the wall of the Ka'bah. The terms of a family's slow starvation were posted at the House, where anyone in Makkah could walk past and read them. Nobody took it down.

Makkah lived on the caravan and the pilgrim. To be cut out of the market of that city was not an insult. It was a decision about who would eat.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham and Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zad Al-Ma'ad

layers.title: What Happened
layers.subtitle: What hunger sounded like from outside the pass
layers.content:
Abu Talib took stock of it quietly and decided not to wait to be starved in his own streets. He withdrew to a narrow valley on the eastern outskirts of Makkah — Ash-Shi'b, the pass of Abu Talib. Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib followed him into it.

They were there from Muharram of the seventh year of the mission until the tenth: three years. Al-Mubarakpuri notes that some reports place the beginning later than Muharram, so the exact start is not agreed.

The supply of food was virtually stopped. The idolaters bought up whatever provisions entered Makkah so that nothing could leak through to the pass. The people inside were reduced to eating the leaves of trees and the skins of animals. The crying of small children from hunger could be heard clearly from outside.

Nothing edible reached them except on the few occasions when some compassionate Makkans smuggled in small quantities. In the prohibited months, when hostilities traditionally ceased, the confined came out to buy food arriving from beyond Makkah — and found the price driven up against them until their money could not reach it.

Hakim bin Hizam was once carrying wheat to his aunt Khadijah when Abu Jahl intercepted him in the road and tried to stop him. Only when Al-Bukhtari intervened did the wheat get through.

Abu Talib feared assassination in the dark. He would have the Prophet ﷺ lie down in his own bed while the others were still awake, then move him to a different place once everyone had fallen asleep.

And through all three years the Prophet ﷺ kept walking to the Ka'bah and praying in the open. He used every sacred month and every hajj season to speak to outsiders who came in for trade or pilgrimage.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: Five men circle the House seven times
layers.content:
The pact held for three years, but it never sat easily. The men enforcing it were tied by blood to the people dying inside the pass, and after three years the disagreement inside Makkah could no longer be contained.

Hisham bin Amr had been slipping food to Banu Hashim in secret at night. He went to Zuhair bin Abi Umaiyah Al-Makhzumi and put it to him directly: how do you agree to this treatment of your own uncles, driven into exile? Zuhair pleaded that he was one man and could do nothing. Then he agreed to work with Hisham and build a pressure group.

There came to be five of them: Hisham bin Amr, Zuhair bin Abi Umaiyah, Al-Mut'im bin Adi, Abul-Bukhtari and Zam'ah bin Al-Aswad. They chose to begin at the Sacred House itself.

Zuhair circled the Ka'bah seven times, then turned on the assembly of Makkans sitting there. He told them what they were: men eating well and enjoying their lives while their own kin in Banu Hashim perished of hunger and blockade. He swore he would not stop until the parchment of boycott was torn to pieces and the pact broken on the spot.

Abu Jahl was standing nearby. He answered sharply: it will never be torn.

Zam'ah rounded on him and called him a liar — the pact had been drawn up and written without ever asking their consent. Abul-Bukhtari backed him. Al-Mut'im bin Adi and Hisham bin Amr attested that both men were speaking the truth. Abu Jahl looked at four men lined up against him and understood that the argument had been arranged before he arrived. He tried to close it down by claiming the matter had already been decided elsewhere.

For the first time in three years, the pact had opposition standing up inside the sanctuary.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Ants, a Name, and a sign they walked away from
layers.content:
Abu Talib had been sitting in a corner of the Masjid through all of it. He came forward and told them why he was there. A revelation had reached his nephew: ants had eaten away every part of the document that carried injustice and aggression, and had left only the parts that bore the Name of Allah.

Then he made them an offer no one could call unfair. If my nephew's word proves false, I will hand him over to you myself. If it proves true, you withdraw and cancel your boycott. The Makkans agreed that the proposition was sound.

Al-Mut'im bin Adi went to inspect the parchment. He found it eaten away by ants. Nothing was left of it except the place where the Name of Allah was written.

The declaration was cancelled. The Prophet ﷺ and the people of the two clans came out of Ash-Shi'b and went home.

No ayah is recorded as having been sent down about the pact itself. Al-Mubarakpuri instead reads over the episode a verse of Surah Al-Qamar, because Quraysh had just been handed the one thing they had spent thirteen years demanding — a sign they could go and verify with their own eyes — and had turned from it: «وَإِن يَرَوْا آيَةً يُعْرِضُوا وَيَقُولُوا سِحْرٌ مُّسْتَمِرٌّ» — 'And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: passing magic.' (54:2)

The account of the ants comes through the sirah reports carried by Ibn Hisham and by Ibn Al-Qayyim in Zad Al-Ma'ad. What it settled was narrow and legal: the blockade was over. What it did not settle was anything at all about their belief. They saw the parchment. They went home. Nothing in them changed.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 54:2 — «وَإِن يَرَوْا آيَةً يُعْرِضُوا وَيَقُولُوا سِحْرٌ مُّسْتَمِرٌّ» 'And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: passing magic'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham and Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zad Al-Ma'ad

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: The pact broke; the pressure did not
layers.content:
Quraysh cancelled the boycott and went straight back to the atrocities. The document was gone. Nothing structural had changed.

Abu Talib walked out of the valley at around eighty years old, victorious and finished. Persistent illness and physical weakness took hold of him almost immediately. Reports differ on when he died: Al-Mubarakpuri prefers Rajab of the tenth year of prophethood, six months after the pact was cancelled, and notes another report placing it in Ramadan, days before Khadijah.

Quraysh could see him failing. They also feared the disgrace the other Arabs would fasten on them if they moved against the Prophet ﷺ the moment his protector was dead. So they sent a delegation of twenty-five men to Abu Talib's sickroom — Utbah bin Rabi'ah, Shaybah bin Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl bin Hisham, Umaiyah bin Khalaf and Abu Sufyan bin Harb among them. They praised the old man, then made their proposal: we will not interfere in his religion if he does not interfere in ours.

Abu Talib called his nephew in and put it to him. The Prophet ﷺ answered with a counter-offer — one word that would give them mastery over the Arabs and the non-Arabs. Abu Jahl swore they would grant it and ten times more. Name the word. He said: that you testify there is no deity worthy of worship but Allah, and dissociate yourselves from everything you worship besides Him.

They clapped their hands in ridicule and walked out. Allah sent down Surah Sad, including: «أَجَعَلَ الْآلِهَةَ إِلَٰهًا وَاحِدًا إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَشَيْءٌ عُجَابٌ» (38:5)

Carry this out of the valley. A boycott is not built to change your mind. It is built to make you negotiate your belief down to a size you can survive on. Three years of leaves and animal skins did not shave one word off the message, and the moment food was available again the offer came anyway — smaller, politer, and asking for the same thing.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 38:5 — «أَجَعَلَ الْآلِهَةَ إِلَٰهًا وَاحِدًا إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَشَيْءٌ عُجَابٌ» 'Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed this is a curious thing'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham and At-Tabari's Tafsir

quiz.prompt: Where was the document of boycott placed once it had been written?

options.text: Buried beneath the Ka'bah as a binding oath
Affixed to the wall of the Ka'bah
Kept in Dar an-Nadwa, the house of assembly
Read aloud at Mina at each pilgrimage season

quiz.scholar_reflection: The terms of a starvation order were posted at the House of Allah. Everyone in Makkah could read them on their way to worship.

quiz.prompt: How long did Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib remain confined in Ash-Shi'b?

options.text: One year
Three years
Seven years
Ten years

quiz.scholar_reflection: From Muharram of the seventh year of the mission to the tenth. Al-Mubarakpuri notes that some reports place the start later, so the exact beginning is not agreed.

quiz.prompt: What were the people in the valley reduced to eating?

options.text: Barley bought at ordinary market price
The leaves of trees and the skins of animals
Provisions sent to them from Abyssinia
Meat left over from the sacrifices at the Ka'bah

quiz.scholar_reflection: The crying of the children from hunger was audible from outside the pass. Makkah heard it for three years.

quiz.prompt: What did Al-Mut'im bin Adi find when he went to inspect the parchment?

options.text: It had been removed and hidden by Abu Jahl
It had been eaten by ants, with only the part bearing the Name of Allah left
It was intact, and he tore it up himself
It had been rewritten with harsher terms

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham and Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zad Al-Ma'ad
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Talib had staked his nephew's life on the claim: hand him over if the word proves false. Al-Mut'im walked over and looked.

quiz.prompt: When the delegation of twenty-five came to Abu Talib's sickroom offering mutual non-interference, what did the Prophet ﷺ ask of them in exchange for mastery over the Arabs and non-Arabs?

options.text: That they stop persecuting the weak among the believers
That they testify there is no deity worthy of worship but Allah and abandon all others
That they permit him to preach freely at the Ka'bah
That they return the property of those who had emigrated

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Jahl swore to grant the word and ten times more before he had heard what it was. When he heard it, they clapped their hands and left.

quiz.prompt: For all three years of the blockade the Prophet ﷺ kept walking out to the Ka'bah and praying in the open. What do you make of that choice?

options.text: It was defiance — a refusal to let them think the siege was working
It was not a statement at all, only worship continuing as normal under abnormal conditions
It kept the message in front of the very people trying to starve it out
It proved the blockade had no reach over the one thing it existed to stop

quiz.slider_label: How much of your practice would survive three years of pressure?
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was hungry, cut off, and hunted at night. The sirah records that nothing about his prayer or his preaching was suspended for it.

quiz.prompt: The pact was broken by five men — Hisham, Zuhair, Al-Mut'im, Abul-Bukhtari and Zam'ah — not one of whom was a Muslim at the time. What does that tell you?

options.text: Allah moves people who do not share your belief to act on your behalf
Conscience is not the exclusive property of the believing
Kinship and public shame accomplished what thirteen years of argument had not
The Muslims were never as alone in that city as the pact was designed to make them feel

quiz.slider_label: How much do you expect from people outside your own circle?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Mut'im bin Adi later gave the Prophet ﷺ armed protection on his return from Ta'if, and died a disbeliever. Both facts are in the sirah.

quiz.prompt: Hungry children could be heard from outside the pass, and only a few Makkans ever smuggled food in. Which fact sits heaviest with you?

options.text: That children went hungry for three years in a city with food in it
That most of Makkah heard it and carried on
That a few risked themselves anyway, and it was not enough to end it
That Abu Jahl stood in the road personally to stop wheat reaching Khadijah

quiz.slider_label: Where do you actually stand — with the few, or with the many?
quiz.scholar_reflection: Hisham bin Amr enforced the pact by day and broke it by night for three years. Eventually the night work turned into organised opposition.

quiz.prompt: Quraysh were handed exactly what they had been demanding — a sign they could go and verify — and they verified it, cancelled the pact, and believed nothing. Why?

options.text: They never wanted evidence; they wanted the message gone
A sign can settle a fact without touching what a person is unwilling to give up
They had too much invested in the old order to follow the evidence anywhere
Belief was never the thing standing in the way — pride was

quiz.slider_label: How much would fresh evidence really change in you?
quiz.citation: Quran 54:2 — 'And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: passing magic'
quiz.scholar_reflection: They walked to the wall of the Ka'bah, examined a parchment eaten by ants, and went home unchanged. The Qur'an had already described the mechanism.

quiz.prompt: The final offer was leave our religion alone and we will leave yours. On paper it ends the persecution outright. How do you read the refusal?

options.text: It was a genuinely fair offer, and refusing it cost the believers years of further suffering
Accepting meant treating tawhid as one option among many, which it cannot be
He did not negotiate at all — he answered an offer of coexistence with an invitation
It would have preserved the community and dissolved the reason the community existed

quiz.slider_label: What would you have answered in that sickroom?
quiz.citation: Quran 38:1-7 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: His uncle was dying, his clan was starved, and the men in the room controlled the city. He answered by asking for more than they offered, not less.
